extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and researchers of classical mechanics and history of science (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted section of Newton's Principia containing theorems and propositions about fluid pressure/density and the motion/resistance of pendulums (cycloidal motion). Includes propositions, cases, corollaries and scholia with geometric demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases 3–7: equality of pressure in spherical parts and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Cas. 3. Dico præterea quod diversarum partium sphæricarum æqualis sit pressio. ... Cas. 4. Dico jam quod fluidi partes omnes ubiq; premuntur æqualiter. ... Cas. 5. Cum igitur fluidi pars quælibet GHI in fluido reliquo tanquam in vase claudatur, & undique prematur æqualiter, partes autem ejus se mutuo æqualiter premant & quiescant inter se; manifestum est quod Fluidi cujuscunque GHI, quod undique premitur æqualiter, partes omnes se mutuo premunt æqualiter, & quiescunt inter se. ... Cas. 6. Igitur si Fluidum illud in vase non rigido claudatur, & undique non prematur æqualiter, cedet idem pressioni fortiori, per Definitionem Fluiditatis. ... Cas. 7. Ideoque in vase rigido Fluidum non sustinebit pressionem fortiorem ex uno latere quam ex alio, sed eidem cedet, idq; in momento temporis, quia latus vasis rigidum non persequitur liquorem cedentem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding explanation and corollaries: from these cases Newton deduces that in a rigid vessel fluid cannot sustain a greater pressure on one side than another and that pressure equalizes (with no local motion) by the opposing wall yielding; if the vessel is not rigid the fluid yields to the stronger pressure. Corollaries state that motion of fluid parts due to an externally applied pressure cannot change unless the external surface shape changes or internal parts change relative mobility; and if pressure does not change internal form or position of immersed bodies if they cannot be compressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. XIX (selected): behavior of submerged bodies and comparative gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1–9: deductions include (1) the bottom is not urged by the whole weight of the fluid but only by the part described in Prop. XX; (2) at equal distances from the center pressure is the same whether surface pressed is parallel, perpendicular, or oblique to the horizon and independent of tortuous channels; (3) heavy fluid parts do not acquire motion from pressure of incumbent weight, excluding condensation effects; (4) a body of same specific gravity submerged will neither ascend nor descend nor change shape by pressure alone; (5) bodies more specifically heavy than contiguous fluid will sink and those lighter will ascend in proportion to the gravity difference; (6) distinction between absolute (true) gravity and comparative (apparent) gravity in fluids and air, and related remarks on folk judgments of 'heavy' and 'light'; (7) results generalize to any centripetal forces; (8) if the medium exerts centripetal force, differences give rise to centrifugal or centripetal effects; (9) fluids compressing immersed systems do not change internal positions unless internal condensation or medium resistance occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries elaborate physical consequences: buoyancy explanation, the concept of apparent vs absolute weight, generalization to other centripetal forces (e.g., magnetic analogy), and statement that immersion under uniform pressure preserves bodies' external shapes and internal relative positions unless compression (condensation) is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XX (Theor. XIV): pressure on a spherical bottom equals weight of a cylinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Fluidi Sphærici, & in æqualibus a centro distantiis homogenei, fundo sphærico concentrico incumbentis partes singulæ versus centrum totius gravitent; sustinet fundum pondus Cylindri, cujus basis æqualis est superficiei fundi, & altitudo eadem quæ Fluidi incumbentis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration: subdivide the fluid into many concentric spherical layers (orbs); each layer exerts pressure on the one below; pressures add in arithmetic series so that the pressure on the bottom is not the whole weight but equals the weight of a cylinder whose base equals the bottom area and whose height equals the fluid depth. Corollaries: (1) the bottom supports only that described part of the weight, remainder being sustained by arch-like fluid shape; (2) at equal distances from center pressure is constant regardless of orientation of the pressed surface and regardless of tortuous passages within the fluid; (3) heavy fluid parts do not acquire motion from pressure of the incumbent weight (excluding condensation); (4) submerged bodies of the same specific gravity remain unchanged by pressure (do not sink or rise or change shape) unless condensation can occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXI (Theor. XV): continuity of density when density proportional to compression and gravity inverse to distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sit Fluidi cujusdam densitas compressioni proportionalis, & partes ejus a vi centripeta distantiis suis a centro reciproce proportionali deorsum trahantur: dico quod si distantiæ illæ sumantur continue proportionales, densitates fluidi in iisdem distantiis erunt etiam continue proportionales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction and demonstration: erect perpendiculars at points corresponding to densities; if specific gravities vary continuously and distances are in continuous proportion, then resulting densities are also continuously proportional. Corollary gives a geometric method using a hyperbola and areas to determine density at any intermediate point given two densities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXII (Theor. XVI): geometric progression of densities when distances are in a 'musical' (geometric) progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Sit Fluidi cujusdam densitas compressioni proportionalis, & partes ejus a gravitate quadratis distantiarum suarum a centro reciproce proportionali deorsum trahantur: dico quod si distantiæ sumantur in progressione Musica, densitates Fluidi in his distantiis erunt in progressione Geometrica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstration uses hyperbola areas: if distances from center are in a geometric progression and the gravity acting on particles is proportional to inverse-square (or more generally to any power rule as discussed in the scholium), then densities follow a geometric progression. Corollary: given two densities one can obtain density at any other using hyperbolic-area construction. Scholium generalizes to other laws where gravity varies with different powers of distance and relates to how density responds to various compression laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIII (Theor. XVII): elastic fluid composed of mutually repelling particles
rubrics_metrics.description: Particulæ viribus quæ sunt reciproce proportionales distantiis centrorum suorum se mutuo fugientes componunt Fluidum Elasticum, cujus densitas est compressioni proportionalis. Et vice versa, si Fluidi ex particulis se mutuo fugientibus compositi densitas sit ut compressio, vires centrifugæ particularum sunt reciproce proportionales distantiis centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by considering compression in nested cubes and relating pressures to densities; shows equivalence between inverse-distance law of repulsion between particles and a macroscopic law where pressure (and thus density under compression) is proportional to compression. Scholium: generalizes to other inverse-power laws, yielding different algebraic relations between density and compression. Newton notes the physical question whether real elastic fluids are made of such mutually repelling particles and gives magnetic attraction as an analogous example where force is effectively localized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIV (Theor. XVIII): mass (quantity of matter) in suspended bodies related to weight and square of oscillation periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitates materiæ in corporibus funependulis, quorum centra oscillationum a centro suspensionis æqualiter distant, sunt in ratione composita ex ratione ponderum & ratione duplicata temporum oscillationum in vacuo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: using Newton's second law concept and proportionality between generated velocity, driving force, time and inverse of mass, Newton shows that for pendula of equal length the masses are as the weights times the squares of their periods in vacuum. Corollaries: (1) if times equal, masses proportional to weights; (2) if weights equal, masses proportional to squares of times; (3) other algebraic relations follow (weights reciprocal to squares of times when masses equal); (4) relation to pendulum length since square of period proportional to length; (5) general formula: mass ∝ weight × (time)^2 × 1/length; (6) in a resisting medium replace absolute weight by comparative weight in that medium; (7) experimental remark that measured masses are proportional to their weights under most accurate experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXV (Theor. XIX): pendula resisted in proportion to time-momenta oscillate in a cycloid
rubrics_metrics.description: Corpora Funependula quæ in Medio quovis resistuntur in ratione momentorum temporis, quæque in ejusdem gravitatis specificæ Medio non resistente moventur, oscillationes in Cycloide eodem tempore peragunt, & arcuum partes proportionales simul describunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance is proportional to the moments of time (i.e., a particular modeled linear-in-time resistance), then pendula that would oscillate in a cycloid in vacuum still perform isochronous oscillations and describe proportional arc parts under the same time intervals even in the resisting medium. Corollary: the point of maximum speed in a resisting medium is shifted from the geometric lowest point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVI (Theor. XX): isochronism of cycloidal oscillations when resistance ∝ velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporum Funependulorum, quæ resistuntur in ratione velocitatum, oscillationes in Cycloide sunt Isochronæ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance is proportional to velocity, then cycloidal oscillations remain isochronous: velocities and arc increments remain proportional to the whole arcs, so bodies starting together describe corresponding arcs and return simultaneously. The proposition provides a general argument that if velocities are at some instant proportional to the whole arcs, then they remain so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVII (Theor. XXI): effect when resistance ∝ velocity^2 (approximate relation of period differences to arcs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora Funependula resistuntur in duplicata ratione velocitatum, differentiæ inter tempora oscillationum in Medio resistente ac tempora oscillationum in ejusdem gravitatis specificæ Medio non resistente, erunt arcubus oscillando descriptis proportionales, quam proxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If resistance is proportional to the squares of velocities, then the differences between oscillation times in the resisting medium and their times in vacuum are approximately proportional to the arcs traversed. Corollaries: (1) measured times in resisting medium can be used to infer times in vacuum; (2) shorter oscillations are more nearly isochronous and the effect of resistance on time is less for small arcs; also discussion of how medium motion influences effective resistance and period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVIII (Theor. XXII): relation between resistance and arc excess in cycloidal oscillation when resistance ∝ time-moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpus Funependulum in Cycloide oscillans resistitur in ratione momentorum temporis, erit ejus resistentia ad vim gravitatis ut excessus arcus descensu toto descripti supra arcum ascensu subsequente descriptum, ad penduli longitudinem duplicatam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cycloidal pendulum experiences resistance proportional to time-moments, then the resistance relates to gravity as the excess of the total descent arc over the subsequent ascent arc, divided by twice the pendulum length. The proof constructs small increments and relates velocity loss due to resistance to corresponding arc differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXIX (Prob. VII): finding resistance at each point when resistance ∝ velocity^2
rubrics_metrics.description: Posito quod corpus in Cycloide oscillans resistitur in duplicata ratione velocitatis: invenire resistentiam in locis singulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses a hyperbola and areas: choose a line and hyperbola so that hyperbolic areas represent the descending and ascending arcs and momenta; then resistance at a given point is given (in the proposition) by a certain difference of hyperbolic areas divided by another area (explicit formula given in proof). Corollaries: (1) resistance at the lowest point expressed as a ratio of hyperbolic areas; (2) maximum resistance when certain area ratios are extreme; (3) method yields velocities at individual points (velocity ∝ square-root of resistance ratio), though the calculus is intricate. Newton notes the computation is difficult and introduces the next proposition as a more general and practically accurate substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX (Theor. XXIII): approximation expressing arc differences and areas for resistance representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Si recta aB æqualis sit Cycloidis arcui quem corpus oscillando describit, & ad singula ejus puncta D erigantur perpendicula DK, quæ sint ad longitudinem Penduli ut resistentia corporis in arcus punctis correspondentibus ad vim gravitatis: dico quod differentia inter arcum descensu toto descriptum, & arcum ascensu toto subsequente descriptum, ducta in arcuum eorundem semisummam, æqualis erit areæ BKaB a perpendiculis omnibus DK occupatæ, quamproxime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposition offers an approximate geometric relation: take a straight line equal to the cycloidal arc and erect perpendiculars proportional to resistances; then the area under those perpendiculars approximates (when multiplied by semisum of arcs) the difference between descent and subsequent ascent arcs. The proof relates infinitesimal changes of velocity and arc increments and uses geometric constructions (semicircles, perpendiculars) to represent velocities and resistance-induced decrements.
